Learning Objectives
Describe the technique for targeted muscle reinnervation.
Describe the role of targeted muscle reinnervation for myoelectric prosthetic function and
neuroma management and prevention.
List the surgical approaches, relevant anatomy, and surgical technique for targeted muscle
reinnervation based on amputation level.
Background
Limb amputation is a life-changing event. Amputation may result from trauma in a young,
otherwise healthy patient population or because of tumor resection or a comorbid medical

condition, such as diabetes mellitus or peripheral vascular disease.1 Although an amputation
may be devastating functionally, it also may be life-saving (Resource 1).
In 2024, an estimated 2.3 million individuals in the United States were living with limb loss, 9%
of which involved the upper limb.2 This number is predicted to double by 2060.2 Worldwide,
more than 1 million extremity amputations are performed every year.2 Most amputations are
related to diabetes mellitus and vascular disease.
More than 1,700 US military service members have a major limb amputation, and many US
military service members have multiple amputations.3,4 Service member injuries often result
from high-energy improvised explosive devices, and 17% of injuries involve the upper
extremity.3,4 Substantial rates of troubling neuroma symptoms, residual limb and phantom
limb pain, notable pain and activity intolerance, and difficulty returning to life roles and
employment are similar in the military and civilian experience.5-8
Increased attention from the federal government and the public, availability of increased
funding, and increased attention aimed at improving quality of life and function among
individuals with a major limb amputation has catalyzed improvements in extremity
prostheses, making them more lightweight, durable, and functional.9
Despite these advances, many amputees make little use of a prostheses because of
discomfort, the weight of the prosthesis, and lack of intuitive prosthetic control, which
prevents them from readily performing activities of daily living10 (Resource 2).
Overview
Targeted muscle reinnervation (TMR) is the transfer of amputated nerves to nearby muscle
targets in the limb or chest wall.
The neurotized, or reinnervated, muscle can produce an easily detectable myoelectric signal.
This signal can be sensed and used to control a function native to the transferred nerve. This
may lead to more intuitive prosthetic control, corresponding with a nerve’s premorbid
function.
The indications of TMR have expanded not only to improve functional control of prostheses
but also to limit pain from cut nerve endings and residual limb and phantom pain.


TMR is a surgical technique originally developed to address inherently poor prosthetic
acceptance rates. TMR allows patients to overcome the limitations of body-powered
prostheses and maximize the expanding capabilities of myoelectric prosthetic devices.
The use of TMR was reported in a shoulder disarticulation amputee in 2004,
subsequently expanded to the transhumeral level, and currently is also performed in the
lower extremity.11-15 In simple terms, TMR is the transfer of amputated nerves to nearby
muscle targets in the limb or chest wall. The neurotized, or reinnervated, muscle can
produce an easily detectable myoelectric signal that can control a function native to the
transferred nerve, considered to be a more intuitive control corresponding to the nerve’s
premorbid function. For example, in a patient with a transhumeral amputation, transfer
of the median nerve can produce a closed hand function, and the radial nerve can
produce an open hand function. TMR produces reliable rates of reinnervation and
increases the number of intuitively controlled muscle signals by serving as a biologic
amplifier. This neural prosthesis interface allows for simultaneous functionality of
myoelectric prostheses with multiple degrees of freedom.16
TMR has increased application in upper and lower extremity amputation levels. The
indications of TMR have expanded to not only improve functional control of prostheses
but also address problems of neuroma formation and residual limb and phantom
pain.17-20 Motor control potential of amputated nerves is preserved for years and
possibly decades after amputation; this means that TMR technique can be used in the
acute setting and as a reconstructive technique many decades after an amputation.21-24
Advancing technologic improvements in myoelectric prostheses and their computer-
controlled algorithms have the potential to expand the upper limit of functional
capability potential for amputees.22
TMR for Myoelectric Prostheses
Between 4 and 7 months typically are required for the target muscles to become reinnervated.
A myoelectric process then interprets the electromyographic (EMG) signal patterns and
translates them into specific motions, allowing for intuitive control of the prosthesis.
Computer algorithms for myoelectric prostheses, called advanced pattern recognition, allow
for simultaneous motions in multiple planes intuitively directed by the amputee.


TMR for Myoelectric Prostheses
TMR has been successful in producing detectable and functionally useful amplified EMG
signals if performed in patients with shoulder disarticulations and transhumeral
amputations.15,16 In traditional nerve transfers, the desired outcome is a muscle
contraction that can act against gravity, whereas TMR requires only a detectable EMG
signal to produce specific movements of the prosthesis based on pattern recognition.
Typically, between 4 and 7 months are required for the target muscles to become
reinnervated.16 A myoelectric process then interprets the EMG signal patterns and
translates them into specific motions. This process allows for intuitive control of the
prosthesis. The patient need only think of the desired motion, which then translates into
an amplified EMG signal that produces the intended motion from the prosthesis.13
Advanced pattern recognition controls of the prosthesis also allow for simultaneous
motions in multiple planes.25,26 For example, in patients with a transradial amputation,
hand grasp patterns are produced that more closely replicate the complex motions
important for prehension compared what that currently possible with conventional
myoelectric prostheses.27
One of the greatest limitations that persist in current prostheses is the lack of sensory
feedback. Visual feedback is required to use the prosthesis without proprioception.14
TMR also may improve sensory feedback. Some patients who have undergone TMR have
experienced sensory reinnervation in a cutaneous distribution consistent with the
pattern of nerve transfers.28 As haptic feedback technologies advance, this sensory
reintegration with or without deliberate targeted sensory reinnervation may be used to
provide sensory feedback through the prosthesis, and to create a feedback loop of
motor and sensory inputs and outputs that more closely approximate a non-amputated
limb.27
TMR for Neuroma Control and Prevention
At the end of a cut nerve, regeneration facilitated by Schwann cells, in the absence of a normal
distal nerve scaffold, results in a disorganized nerve ending that may be painful or

hypersensitive.
By organizing the nerve ending to connect to muscle, TMR may have a secondary benefit of
limiting nociception arising from disorganized healing of a cut nerve.

TMR for Neuroma Control and Prevention
Nerve regeneration, facilitated by Schwann cells, in the absence of a normal distal nerve
scaffold results in a disorganized nerve ending (neuroma) that may be painful.17
Residual limb pain because of neuroma formation and phantom limb pain are other well
described sequelae of major limb amputations, reported in as many as 25% of residual
limbs in the US population.20 Somewhat serendipitously, TMR has been associated with
lower pain intensity. A retrospective review of 15 patients undergoing upper extremity
TMR for neuroma pain after initial amputation reported complete resolution of pain in
all but one patient.17 A follow-on preclinical animal model confirmed that transection of
neuromas and implantation of nerves into normal muscle organizes nerve regeneration
by providing the nerve something to do.29 More recently, a randomized, prospective trial
comparing 28 patients assigned to standard amputation treatment versus TMR found
that TMR was associated with a two to three point reduction that was not statistically
significant with regard to residual limb pain but was significant with regard to phantom
limb pain.19 A prospective cohort of patients with notable persistent pain after major
limb amputation who declined randomization in the trial described experienced 1-year
decreases in residual limb pain from 6.4 to 3.6 and a mean decrease from 6.0 to 3.6 on a
scale of 0 to 10.30 A multicenter retrospective cohort study comparing 51 patients who
underwent immediate TMR at the time of major limb amputation and 438 unselected
major limb amputees reported a pain-free rate in the TMR cohort twice that of the non-
TMR cohort, or a 45% percent reduction in the TMR cohort compared with an
approximately 20% reduction in the non-TMR cohort.20 These and other studies have
established TMR as a surgical treatment option to alleviate residual limb pain and
phantom limb pain in patients with an upper or lower extremity limb amputation.18,31
This improvement in pain also may translate to a higher rate of prosthesis acceptance
because the patient is able to tolerate pressure against the residual limb, resulting in
greater acceptance and use of the prosthesis.

Principles of TMR
The surgical technique for TMR has evolved over the course of the past 2 decades, and several
principles of the procedure are recommended to ensure success:
The donor nerve should be an unused peripheral nerve without current function.
The donor nerve should have no potential impairment in function, such as the presence of a
spinal cord injury or brachial plexopathy.
The donor nerve should be of adequate length to reach target muscle motor nerves.
The target muscle should be redundant and should not compromise native function if
recruited for myoelectric functional improvement.
Coaptation should occur as close as possible to the motor end plate target; this ensures less
distance to reinnervation and will minimize time to neuralization of the healthy tissue
envelope.
The coaptation must be tension-free to optimize the transfer and sprouting fascicles into the
distal motor end plate.
If TMR is to be used for myoelectric control:
Recipient muscle size should be at least 3 to 5 mm in diameter and approximately 1 cm
thick to ensure amplification of motor control signal.
Minimal soft tissue between muscle and skin will facilitate signal detection.
Muscle targets should be spaced out to minimize myoelectric cross talk or overlapping
myoelectric signals.
Surgical Indications, Patient Selection, and Planning
TMR may be indicated for any amputation level.
History of spinal cord or complete brachial plexus injuries generally is considered a strong
contraindication.
Age does not appear to be a major factor in TMR success rates.
Functional TMR for patients with bilateral upper extremity amputation must be considered
and weighed against the option for hand transplantation.

Surgical Indications, Patient Selection, and Planning

TMR may be indicated for any amputation level in which the distal limb cannot be
salvaged or in patients who are undergoing elective amputation because of unsuccessful
limb salvage attempts. TMR also may be indicated as a secondary procedure in patients
with a previous amputation who have pain ascribed to a neuroma or a desire for greater
prosthetic control. The procedure may be indicated in select patients without an
amputation, typically performed for painful neuromas; however, the surgeon must
balance the potential for pain alleviation against the potential for loss of function.
History of spinal cord or complete brachial plexus injury generally is considered a strong
contraindication to functional TMR. Whether any history of generalized neuropathy
precludes this procedure remains unclear; however, any preexisting condition of the
nervous system may result in less optimal results. Although nerve repair and
reconstruction outcomes are correlated with patient age, age does not appear to be a
major factor in TMR success rates.
A multidisciplinary approach is vital for the success of the procedure. Psychology,
physical medicine and rehabilitation, occupational therapy, prosthetics, and social work
are crucial specialties to include throughout the preoperative and postoperative course.
Patients must be willing to undergo extensive occupational therapy postoperatively.
Patients typically are fit with a body-powered or simple myoelectric prosthesis for
several months while waiting for the TMR to mature and reinnervation to occur (Figure
1). Cost and, as a result, healthcare coverage for prostheses must be considered. The
recent military conflicts have driven an influx in government funding to research and
development of upper extremity prostheses; however, such prostheses remain costly for
the civilian population.9
Future treatment options, such as vascularized composite allotransplantation (ie, hand
transplantation) may be considered by the surgical team and discussed with the patient.
Careful consideration of TMR, particularly in patients with bilateral upper extremity
amputation, is important because TMR shortens the available nerve for subsequent
transplantation.

Surgical Timing and Limb Optimization

Surgical Timing and Limb Optimization
TMR surgery can be performed at the time of amputation and as a reconstructive
technique many years after an amputation. Motor control potential of amputated nerves
is preserved for years and possibly decades after amputation.21-24 Acute TMR is not
recommended in certain situations based on injury patterns, surgeon or facility
capability, or patient factors This includes dysvascular or infected limbs in which the
ultimate success of the initial amputation may be compromised by a longer procedure
or by residual infection or nonviability and scenarios in which surgical expediency is
necessary for the patient’s best interests.20 The initial treating surgeon must not only be
cognizant of modern principles of amputation surgery at any level but also consider the
possibility of future reconstructive options, including TMR, to optimize future limb
function and manage a painful neuroma. Although general amputation management is
not the focus of this lesson, three points applicable to TMR are worth highlighting.32,33
First, preservation of limb length may enhance future TMR for functional myoelectric
prosthetic control. Length preservation generally is desirable in the upper extremity
amputee; however, it must be balanced against capacity for wound healing and residual
limb coverage, patient preference, rehabilitation potential, and local prosthetic expertise
and availability. With increasing length and preservation of joints, enhanced positioning
of the terminal extremity and/or prosthetic device in space is achieved, allowing for the
greatest functional result and improved outcomes. For TMR, preserving length may
preserve additional muscle targets for nerve transfer. For example, a long transhumeral
amputation can preserve the brachialis muscle for ulnar nerve transfer, allowing for an
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:46 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004035
9/32

additional intuitive muscle signal for additional wrist or hand myoelectric control. If
residual tissue flaps are inadequate to provide distal amputation coverage below the
elbow, and shortening will diminish prosthetic fitting and functional outcomes,
additional soft-tissue coverage options, including skin grafts and flaps, should be
strongly considered, including the use of microvascular free tissue transfer.
Second, careful attention should be paid to nerve and distal muscle management at the
time of amputation to avoid limiting future reconstructive options, including TMR. All
named sensory and motor nerves should be identified before final amputation closure.
All motor branches to muscle flaps within the surgical field should be preserved to
prevent loss of myoelectric signals and loss of muscle mass important for distal limb
padding and comfort. Similarly, cutaneous nerves to skin flaps required for distal
amputation coverage also should be preserved. All other nerves should undergo
transection, or gentle traction neurectomy, to locate neuromas away from the distal
amputation myodesis or skin closure. Although more aggressive traction neurectomy of
named peripheral nerves was recommended in the past, preservation of additional
nerve length, while preventing more distal exposure of neuromas, may preserve the
ability to perform future TMR or hand transplantation. For similar reasons and because
they are not supported by evidence, the authors of this lesson avoid additional nerve
techniques, such as cauterization, suture ligation, proximal nerve crushing, and
anesthetic injection.
Lastly, stabilizing the muscle-tendon units of the residual limb under physiologic tension
at the time of amputation closure is advised and serves two main purposes. First, and
most applicable to TMR, optimal contractility characteristics of the muscle are preserved,
improving muscle signal quality, maximizing myoelectric prosthesis control, and
secondarily maximizing terminal residual limb control for body-powered prostheses
during initial rehabilitation. Second, it provides robust coverage over the distal bone end,
providing comfortable padding for the prosthetic socket while preventing painful bursa
formation from mobile muscle units that may limit prosthetic acceptance. Myodesis, the
process of attaching muscle-tendon units directly to bone, is the surgical technique that
provides the most stable construct over the distal bone end. This typically is achieved by
suturing the muscle and/or tendon to the bone end, usually through drill tunnels with
the use of braided, nonabsorbable suture or, less commonly, to periosteum. Myoplasty,

attaching agonist muscles to antagonist muscles over the bone end to create physiologic
tension, and myofascial closure, or suturing of muscle and fascia together, may be
indicated if myodesis cannot be achieved, for secondary muscles after primary myodesis
is performed, or to contour remaining muscles before closure. Although no data in the
literature supports the superiority of myodesis over myoplasty, myodesis is
recommended in patients with an upper extremity amputation to provide the most
stable limb, and to best isolate muscle signals and myoelectric prosthetic control.
TMR by Amputation Level
General Considerations
A neurovascular examination identifies the availability of muscle targets and the patient’s
suitability to proceed with TMR.
Radiographs are obtained to assess residual limb length and the presence of heterotopic
ossification.
Tinel testing to identify distal major peripheral nerve neuromas
Mark the location of muscles and nerves intended for transfer, as well as planned incisions, in
the preoperative holding area.
A handheld single-use nerve stimulator is helpful.
Avoid paralyzing anesthetic agents during the procedure.

General Considerations
Surgical planning via a thorough neurovascular examination identifies the availability of
muscle targets and a patient’s suitability to proceed with TMR. Radiographs are obtained
to assess residual limb length and for heterotopic ossification. Although Tinel testing
typically will localize distal major peripheral nerve neuromas, advanced imaging studies,
such as MRI or ultrasonography, may be obtained in patients with considerably distorted
anatomy because of prior trauma or surgery. Electrodiagnostic testing also may be
indicated if concerns exist with regard to proximal nerve injury and the viability of distal
muscle targets for nerve transfer. Marking the location of nerves intended for transfer in
the preoperative holding area via Tinel testing and marking of incisions is advised. This

preoperative marking is especially relevant for transhumeral and transfemoral levels
because the absence of distal bone condyles may distort landmarks after the patient is
positioned and draped on the surgical table.
The procedure is performed in the upper extremity with the patient in the supine
position and the extremity placed on a hand table. The prone or supine position can be
used for lower extremity TMR, depending on the level of amputation managed and any
concomitant revision or reconstructive procedures performed. Although not an absolute
requirement, a tourniquet is recommended to provide a bloodless field during initial
surgical dissection; tourniquet use is especially valuable if substantial fibrosis, scarring,
and/or distorted anatomy is expected. A handheld single-use nerve stimulator is helpful
for identification of nerve-muscle targets and verifies removal of unnecessary motor
nerves if performing the procedure for functional myoelectric control. The authors of
this lesson recommend regional anesthesia as a pain control adjunct; this is performed
by the anesthesia team preoperatively; proximal nerve blockade does not preclude distal
motor unit testing with the use of a nerve stimulator intraoperatively; however,
paralyzing anesthetic agents should be avoided during the procedure, and prolonged
tourniquet use should be avoided before use of a nerve stimulator because it effectively
can degrade after 30 to 45 minutes of tourniquet time.
Surgical Technique for Nerve Transfer
Use an 8-0 or smaller caliber nonabsorbable suture to coapt the recipient motor nerve to the
donor peripheral nerve, with additional 6-0 sutures of the donor nerve to surrounding muscle
epimysium sutures to reinforce the repair.

Surgical Technique for Nerve Transfer
The surgical procedure for nerve coaptation, or transfer, has evolved over time, and no
single surgical technique is superior.12-16,32,34-38 The original description consisted of
division of the motor nerve to the recipient muscle at its insertion to the muscle, and
suture of the amputated large peripheral nerve to the muscle epimysium over the motor
nerve entry point with the use of a 6-0 or 7-0 caliber nonresorbable suture. Currently,

12/32

many surgeons use an 8-0 or smaller caliber nonresorbable suture to coapt the recipient
motor nerve to the donor peripheral nerve, with additional sutures of the donor nerve to
the surrounding muscle epimysium sutures to reinforce the repair. The great number of
fascicles in the donor nerve and the need for only a few fascicles to cross to the target
nerve for a detectable EMG signal to propagate makes this procedure less technically
exacting and allows the nerve transfers to be performed under loupe magnification.
Regardless of technique used, a large peripheral nerve placed in proximity to a motor
end plate will hyper-innervate the muscle target and reliably produce a functional
myoelectric signal. The other motor nerve branches to the target muscles are
transected, with the ends buried away from each other to prevent cross-communication
and to ensure EMG signals from these muscles are from the transferred nerves only. If
the goal is purely to control painful neuromata, this additional step is not required, and a
regenerative peripheral nerve interface (RPNI) also may be used.
Transhumeral Amputation
Donor nerve and muscle targets
Median nerve to the short head of the biceps
Radial nerve to the lateral triceps
Ulnar nerve to the brachialis muscle

Transhumeral Amputation
The rationale and surgical technique for transhumeral TMR is well described.15,28,34,35
TMR was first described for the transhumeral amputation level to address historically
low prosthetic acceptance rates and poor functional outcomes. Transhumeral TMR has
the longest track record reported in the literature and results in reliable rates of muscle
reinnervation and myoelectric prosthetic control. If performed to improve myoelectric
function, the goal of transhumeral TMR is to produce a hand close muscle signal by
transferring the median nerve to a motor nerve to the short head of the biceps muscle,
and a hand open muscle signal via transfer of the radial nerve to a motor nerve to the
lateral head of the triceps. This is performed while protecting motor nerves to the long
head of the biceps and remaining triceps muscles to preserve elbow flexion and

extension. In patients with a long residual limb and brachialis muscle preservation, the
ulnar nerve can be transferred to this muscle to allow a muscle signal for additional wrist
or hand control as indicated. Creation of adipofascial flaps to insert between the biceps
and triceps muscles was recommended in the initial descriptions of transhumeral TMR
to isolate the new muscle signals for myoelectric sensors; however, advanced pattern
recognition algorithms with modern myoelectric prostheses have improved to such a
degree that this step is optional and may not be required.32,39
A distal humerus flexion osteotomy, known as a Marquardt osteotomy, is well described
as an adjunct to TMR to enhance prosthetic suspension. This is a technically demanding
procedure if performed via standard incisions for TMR, possibly requiring additional
distal dissection of the limb terminus, and is associated complications, including
infection, wound dehiscence, nonunion, and hardware complications. The decision to
perform a flexion osteotomy must be individualized to each patient, performed in
discussion with a prosthetist, and should consider whether future reconstructive
procedures to enhance prosthetic suspension, such as osseointegration, are planned.
iThe procedure typically is performed with the patient in the supine position on a
standard surgical table with an attached hand table or board (Figure 2). An anterior
incision is made over the raphe between the heads of the biceps muscle. An
adiopofascial flap approximately 3 to 4 cm in width can then be raised as a proximally
based flap for later insertion between the two heads of the biceps. The muscle typically
can be separated via a combination of gentle blunt dissection, allowing for identification
of the musculocutaneous nerve and its branches to the short and long heads of the
biceps muscles. A handheld nerve stimulator is then used to identify a strong motor
branch to the short head of the biceps muscle, to identify other branches to be
sacrificed, and to ensure preservation of all motor branches to the lateral biceps muscle.
In a longer residual limb, distal motor branches to the brachialis muscle also can be
identified in similar fashion. The median nerve is then found medial to the biceps
muscle, and the ulnar nerve is found medial and posterior to the intermuscular septum.
The distal neuromas do not require excision because they will be deinnervated via
transection of the peripheral nerves proximally; however, dissection must be distal
enough for appropriate nerve length to reach the target muscles. Both nerves are then
mobilized and pass laterally under the short head of the biceps muscle to the space

The radial nerve is then performed via a midline posterior incision in a similar fashion
between the long and lateral heads of the triceps muscles. The radial nerve is identified
deep and traced distally and laterally until adequate length is attained, and the handheld
nerve stimulator is used to identify a good nerve target to the lateral triceps muscle, to
ensure other motor branches to the lateral triceps are sacrificed, and that the long and
medial heads of triceps motor branches are preserved. The radial nerve is then
transferred to the motor branch of the lateral triceps muscle. The adipofascial flaps, if
performed, can then be interposed between the biceps and triceps muscles before
closure, followed by a lightly compressive dressing. A splint is not necessary if only
performing TMR.
Shoulder Disarticulation
Donor nerve and muscle targets
Musculocutaneous nerve to the clavicular head pectoralis muscle
Median nerve to the sternal head pectoralis muscle
Ulnar nerve to the split sternal head pectoralis muscle
Radial nerve to the latissimus dorsi muscle

Shoulder Disarticulation
Shoulder disarticulation-level TMR is a challenge and highly variable because of its
proximity and common association with severe trauma or extensive oncologic
dissection. Donor nerve targets may be too proximal or damaged for transfer, and
motor nerve targets or their muscles may be damaged and unusable, making TMR at this
level far less predictable than at more distal levels.17 The goals for shoulder
disarticulation TMR are to create four new myoelectric signals prioritized in the following
order: elbow flexion, hand closing, hand opening, and elbow extension14,27 (Figure 3).
The common nerve transfers described are transfer of the distal musculocutaneous
remnant to the clavicular head of the pectoralis muscle for elbow flexion, the remnant
median nerve is transferred to the sternal head of the pectoralis major muscle, which
can be split into two separate muscle segments with motor nerves available for transfer,

its motor branch from the thoracodorsal nerve for elbow extension.

The surgical technique is well described and can be performed with or without the
patient under general anesthesia.18,34,35 A transverse incision is placed two
fingerbreadths below the clavicle, and an adipofascial flap may be raised to place
between a split sternal head or between the sternal head and the clavicular head later.
The interval between the sternal head and the clavicular head is developed, exposing the
throacoacromial vascular pedicle and the motor branches to the sternal head, and a self-
retaining retractor is placed. The vascular pedicle is preserved to aid in determining the
sternal head split later. Motor branches from the medial pectoral nerve to the sternal
head are then identified. Motor branches from the lateral pectoral nerve to the clavicular
head can then be identified entering vertically adjacent to the vascular pedicle. The
brachial plexus is found and dissected within the interval between the sternal head and
the clavicular head of the pectoralis major muscles medial or lateral to the pectoralis
minor muscle. The pectoralis minor can be divided, if necessary, for better exposure. The
brachial plexus chords and the distal nerve remnants can then be identified, including
the thoracodorsal nerve, which is aided by the use of a handheld nerve stimulator; care
must be taken to prevent injury to the axillary artery and vein. Nerve transfer is then
performed to targets as previously described.

Donor nerve and muscle targets
Median nerve to the flexor digitorum superficialis or profundus for distal amputations
Median nerve to the pronator teres of the flexor carpi radialis in proximal amputation
Ulnar nerve to the flexor digitorum superficialis, flexor pollicis longus, or flexor carpi ulnaris
(proximal amputation)
Sensory branch of the radial nerve to the local muscle nerve branch or use an RPNI (Figure

Transradial Amputation
Transradial amputation represents the most common level of upper extremity
amputation proximal to the fingers and most frequently is the result of trauma.39
Patients who require transradial amputation are more likely to be young individuals of
working age, which differs from patients with a lower extremity amputation.40 Patients
with a transradial amputation have the highest rate of prosthesis use among patients
with a major upper extremity amputation, and they are the most likely to remain within

the working population41 (Figure 5). Unfortunately, these patients also are the most
likely among those with an upper extremity amputation to suffer from phantom limb
pain and require neuropathic pain medications.7 Techniques for transradial TMR have
been described for myoelectric functional benefit and neuroma control.32,36 The primary
goal of transradial TMR for myoelectric function is to enhance thumb opposition and
pinch and to further improve intuitive intrinsic control of the prosthetic hand.
A midline longitudinal incision typically is used or large volar and dorsal fish-mouth–type
flaps are performed if TMR is performed for acute amputation or if distal amputation
revision is indicated, which is common. The median nerve, the ulnar nerve and its dorsal
sensory branches, the sensory branches of the radial nerve, and the terminal branches
of the lateral and medial antebrachial cutaneous nerves are identified. The median nerve
and the ulnar nerve are transected sharply as distal as possible to provide length for
tension-free reinnervation transfer. If transfer of the superficial branch of the radial
nerve also is planned, this nerve also is transected sharply as distal as possible.
In patients with a longer residual limb, muscle targets for the median nerve are the
flexor digitorum superficialis or profundus; in patients with a more proximal amputation,
the pronator teres and the flexor carpi radialis also can be used. The ulnar nerve can
easily be transferred to the motor branches of the flexor carpi ulnaris or, alternatively,
may be brought under the flexor digitorum superficialis to transfer to a motor branch to
the flexor pollicis longus. In the experience of the authors of this lesson, this transfer has
proven anatomically reliable and provides ulnar nerve animation of a muscle that is
relatively superficial and distal within the terminal residuum. If included, the superficial
branch of the radial nerve can be transferred to the flexor digitorum profundus, the
flexor digitorum superficialis, the extensor carpi radialis longus, or the brachioradialis
muscle. Alternatively, the superficial branch of the radial nerve or any large sensory
nerve can be sutured to a section of denervated muscle to construct an RPNI to avoid
risking unnecessary additional functional muscle denervation or if additional nerve
targets are not available.

Partial Hand Amputation

Partial Hand Amputation
Currently, only case reports of TMR for ray amputation or more extensive partial hand
amputation are reported in the literature;42,43 however, interest in TMR for partial hands
for functional myoelectric prosthetic control and neuroma control is increasing. A recent
cadaver model study identified numerous intrinsic muscle nerve targets from the ulnar
nerve for digital and dorsal sensory nerve transfers.37 Although early results are
promising, additional research is necessary to validate the utility of TMR in this patient
population.

Lower Extremity Amputation
Neuroma control and prevention is the most common indication for TMR in the lower
extremity.
TMR techniques are reported for transfemoral and below-knee amputation levels.

Lower Extremity Amputation
The continued innovation and advancement of lower extremity myoelectric technology
to knee and ankle function, in addition to applications for neuroma control and
prevention, have expanded the application of TMR to lower extremity amputation
levels.34,38,44-46 Numerous recent studies have shown the benefits of TMR in the lower
extremity for neuroma control and phantom limb pain, making this the most common
application of TMR for transfemoral and below-knee amputations.18-20,46
Transfemoral amputation TMR technique was first described for myoelectric prosthetic
control.34,38,45 Although technologic advances in lower extremity myoelectric technology
have not been widely used, the application of TMR for neuroma control continues to
increase. The most common technique involves a posterior midline thigh incision,
developing the plane between the biceps femoris and the semitendinosus muscles,
taking care to preserve all motor branches. The sciatic nerve is identified deep in this
plane and can be divided into its peroneal and tibial trunks, which typically is
straightforward in the midthigh and distal thigh. Typically, the peroneal trunk of the
sciatic nerve will be transferred laterally to the biceps femoris muscles and the tibial
trunk of the sciatic nerve will be transferred to the semitendinosus or, alternatively, the
semimembranosus muscles deeper. Identified sensory nerves, including anterior and
posterior femoral cutaneous nerves, can be transferred to additional motor nerves to
the hamstring muscles, or an RPNI can be formed and placed deep in the muscle
intervals.
TMR for below-knee amputation levels recently has been described.46 If performed at
the same time as the primary amputation, the amputation incision can be used to

to identify the posterior tibial nerve posteriorly, and lateral dissection through the same
incision can be carried out to identify the deep peroneal nerve. The deep peroneal nerve
can be identified laterally anterior to the fibula and coapted to the tibialis anterior,
peroneus longus, peroneus brevis, or medial soleus muscles. The deep peroneal nerve is
found in the posterior compartment of the leg and can be transferred to a motor branch
of the medial or lateral gastrocnemius, tibialis posterior, or medial or lateral soleus
muscles. Identified sensory nerves, including the superficial peroneal, sural, and
saphenous nerves, can be transferred to additional motor nerves to the previously
described muscle targets, or an RPNI can be formed and placed deep in the muscle
intervals.
RPNI and TMR
An RPNI may serve as an adjunct to TMR if more donor nerves are present than available
motor nerves to muscle targets.

RPNI and TMR
RPNI is an alternative surgical technique that has been proposed to improve myoelectric
prosthetic control and management of residual and phantom limb pain. For the
purposes of this discussion of TMR, an RPNI may serve as an adjunct if too few suitable
muscle targets are present for nerve transfer in formal TMR. An RPNI is performed by
implanting the distal transected nerve into a free devascularized muscle graft.47 The
devascularized muscle graft will go through a degenerative/regenerative process
biologically similar to that of skin grafts and support regenerating nerve axons forming
functional connections and minimizing neuroma formation.48,49 Preliminary studies
have shown functional and neuroma pain benefits, with one study reporting a decrease
in neuroma pain in 71% of patients and a reduction in phantom limb pain in 53% of
patients.46 An advantage of preforming TMR at the time of the primary amputation is
that the amputated muscle tissue serves as an excellent donor for the use of an RPNI as

amputation if the primary goal is neuroma control and a large number of sensory nerve
donors are found. Although not the focus of this lesson, any surgeon performing TMR
should be familiar with RPNI techniques.
Postoperative Management
The patient can begin fitting for a body-powered or myoelectric prosthesis after the wound
has completely healed and soft-tissue edema has begun to dissipate, typically within 4 to 6
weeks postoperatively.
A specialized TMR prosthesis is fitted 5 to 6 months postoperatively after clinical and
myoelectric testing confirms reinnervation of the targeted muscle groups.

Postoperative Management
The patient frequently is admitted for soft-tissue elevation and pain control. The patient
is enrolled in physical therapy by postoperative day one to begin range of motion
exercises of the elbow. Antibiotic agents are continued for 24 hours or more after
inpatient surgery or if indicated for a contaminated or infected wound. The patient can
begin fitting for a body-powered or myoelectric prosthesis after the wound has
completely healed and soft-tissue edema has begun to dissipate, typically within 4 to 6
weeks postoperatively. A specialized TMR prosthesis is fitted 5 to 6 months
postoperatively after clinical and myoelectric testing confirms reinnervation of the
targeted muscle groups.33 The procedure is successful if the prosthesis is able to detect
a signal produced by the targeted muscle, demonstrating coaptation and control of the
target muscle by the transferred nerve. Patients undergoing TMR strictly for pain
management can return to their current prosthesis based on any concurrent revision
procedures performed and their postoperative recovery. The patient frequently is
admitted for soft-tissue elevation and pain control. The patient is enrolled in physical

Complications

Complications
The traumatic nature of any amputation may make secondary surgery a challenge
because of altered anatomy and compromised soft-tissue coverage. Despite these
challenges, TMR can be performed safely and reliably, with minimal associated
morbidity. Complications specific to TMR procedures are limited to failure of
reinnervation of the target muscle groups or, theoretically, inadvertent and
unintentional denervation of a native muscle group that was previously used for
myoelectric control. With meticulous dissection and surgical technique, the authors of
this lesson have not yet had a patient experience these complications after TMR.
Summary

Summary
TMR provides an opportunity to improve the functionality of the residual limb after any
major amputation and to improve pain control after amputation compared with
traditional techniques. In the upper extremity, shoulder disarticulation and

transhumeral amputation drastically improves myoelectric function compared with
historic myoelectric controls and body-powered prostheses. In transradial and partial
hand amputation, TMR in combination with RPNI provides intuitive control over the
prosthesis. The lower the amputation level, the greater the degrees of freedom,
potentially allowing for motion that more closely approximates intrinsic motion of the
hand. In the lower extremity, the primary indication for TMR remains neuroma pain
control and management of phantom limb pain; however, functional benefits are
promising. By providing each nerve somewhere to go and something to do, the
incidence of neuroma-related pain may be much lower than that after traditional
amputation techniques. TMR offers an opportunity to improve functional outcomes
while alleviating the considerable complication of neuroma-related pain.
